title: The Flood and the remaking of the human order: Enki's warning through the reed wall, the boat, the deluge, and the permanent limits on humankind

translation.sourceText: Akkadian reconstruction from named scholarly editions (Lambert & Millard 1969, the critical edition; George & Al-Rawi 1996 for the Old Babylonian Sippar witnesses; Foster 2005 Before the Muses 3rd ed.). Line-numbering follows Lambert–Millard 1969 (Tablet III is cited by column: III i–viii); refIds encode the column and line as ATRA-WOH-III:{col}.{line}.
translation.sourceLicense: Best-effort reconstruction; scholarly editions cited as references; English original to this project (CC0-1.0).
translation.sourceUrl: (no openly-licensed digital source — see source-akk-3.json citations; eBL L.1.1 consulted as collation aid only, CC BY-NC, not reproduced)
translation.sourceAccessedVia: Best-effort reconstruction (Lambert–Millard 1969 + George & Al-Rawi 1996 + Foster 2005; eBL L.1.1 collation aid)
translation.verificationStatus: best-effort-reconstruction-pending-verification; sign-by-sign transliteration pending collation against Lambert–Millard 1969 and eBL L.1.1. Tablet III (the Old Babylonian flood tablet of the Ipiq-Aya/Ku-Aya recension) is the best-preserved of the three tablets and is reconstructed more fully here than the fragmentary tablets; the sense of each line is well-attested across the cited editions.
translation.reviewer: approved — all lines + glossary entries defensible; zero lens-leakage (ab3b5f7c).
translation.humanRuling: 2026-07-04: Human-ratified, extending the standing lens-neutral policy to Tablets II-III. The Elohim/ancient-astronaut population-control identification is kept OUT of translation and glossary (proposed-not-committed 'atrahasis-population-control-elohim-frame'), routed to the Explainer 'made-from-the-ground-to-bear-the-labor'. Ratified: eleppu='boat' (not 'ark'); kima zumbi='like flies'. Tablet II refIds normalized to dot form. Verification-pending holds (Tablet II most damaged; sign-collation gate open).

segments.label: Enki warns Atra-ḫasīs through the reed wall — dismantle the house, build the boat, save life (Lambert–Millard III i, curated)

preceding_lacuna.text: The end of Tablet I and all of Tablet II are not reconstructed in this draft: the multiplication of humankind, the clamor that disturbs Enlil, and Enlil's successive attempts to reduce humankind (plague, drought, famine) before the council decrees the Flood (abūbu). Tablet III opens with Enki, oath-bound not to warn a human directly, addressing the reed wall of Atra-ḫasīs's reed hut so that the man overhears.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection: the end of Tablet I and all of Tablet II — the growth of humankind, the clamor, and Enlil's plague, drought, and famine — are not reconstructed in this draft. Tablet III opens with Enki addressing the reed wall.]
"Wall, listen closely to me!

notes.official: Tablet III opens with the oath-loophole. Enki, bound by the *māmītu* (the oath of Tablet II viii) not to warn a human of the Flood directly, addresses the *igāru* 'wall' / *kikkišu* 'reed-fence' of Atra-ḫasīs's hut so the man 'overhears' (III i 11–12) — keeping the letter of the oath, as he will later plead (III vi 13–14, 'I did not reveal the command of the gods'). This talking-through-the-wall device is a cross-corpus flood-trope (Sumerian Flood Story; famously Gilgamesh XI 21–22, *kikkiš kikkiš igār igār*), carried by the central `iz-zi-da-kikkish-...` and `ea-warning-...` entries; the specific Akkadian wording is anchored in the overlay `igaru-kikkishu-reed-wall-oath-loophole-atrahasis`, with central Akkadian-side `appliesTo` activation flagged.

i18n.en: reed wall, attend to all my words!
Dismantle the house, build a boat!

notes.official: *uqur bīta bini eleppa* 'dismantle the house, build a boat' (III i 13). *eleppu* (CAD E 90) is the ordinary Akkadian word for 'boat, ship'; the translation renders 'a boat', deliberately avoiding the anachronistic 'ark' (an English word tied to the Vulgate *arca* and the Hebrew *tēbāh*). The central `ma-gur-eleppu-tevah-flood-vessel-cross-corpus` files *eleppu* with Sumerian *ma-gur* 'great-boat' and Hebrew *tēbāh*; its wohChoice ('the great boat') is tuned to the Sumerian, so for plain Akkadian *eleppu* the Editor keeps 'boat' and flags the Akkadian-side `appliesTo` activation for the central step. The vessel is to be roofed over 'like the Apsû' and sealed with *kupru* pitch (i 17, 21, 29) — a cube-like covered barge, not the later long-hulled ark.

i18n.en: Spurn possessions and keep life alive!

notes.official: *makkūra zērma napišta bulliṭ* 'spurn possessions and keep life alive' (III i 14). *napištu* is 'life, living being' and *bulliṭ* is the D-imperative of *balāṭu* 'keep alive, preserve' — a collective charge to rescue the seed of life (the family and the living creatures loaded in ii 18–21), not merely 'save your own life'. The same root frames the aftermath (vi 9, 'where did *napištu* escape?'; vi 18, 'because of life I brought it out'). Compare Genesis 6:19–20 (*lĕhaḥăyôt* 'to keep alive') and 7:3 (*lĕḥayyôt zeraʿ* 'to keep seed alive'). See `napishtu-bullit-save-life-flood-instruction-atrahasis`.

i18n.en: The boat that you shall build —
let her breadth and her length be equal.
Roof her over like the Apsû,
so that Shamash may not see within her.
Let her be roofed above and below.
Let her tackle be very strong;
let the pitch be tough, let it give strength.
I myself will rain down upon you

notes.official: Enki's promise 'I myself will rain down upon you an abundance of birds, a profusion of fish' (III i 22–23) is the double-edged assurance flagged by the central `ea-warning-deception-misadvice-test-crux-cross-corpus`: *ušaznanakkum* 'I will rain upon you' names, ambiguously, both the promised bounty and the coming deluge (the famous *kukku*/*kibtu* wordplay of Gilgamesh XI 43–47, where the same 'rain' is prosperity to the townsfolk and destruction in fact). Rendered straight; the crux is documented in the central entry, not editorialized into the line.

i18n.en: an abundance of birds, a profusion of fish.

segments.label: Atra-ḫasīs builds and loads the boat; the elders, the banquet, the boarding, and the sealing of the door (Lambert–Millard III ii, curated)

preceding_lacuna.text: Lines III i 24 to III ii 9 (Atra-ḫasīs's reply to Enki, the mustering of the carpenter and the reed-worker, and the details of the boat's construction) are not reconstructed here.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection: the construction details and the mustering of the craftsmen (III i 24 – III ii 9) are not reconstructed in this draft.]
Atra-ḫasīs received the command.

notes.official: The hero's name recurs (III ii 10, 'Atra-ḫasīs received the command'); *Atra(m)-ḫasīs* 'exceedingly wise' (*atra* + *ḫasīsu*). Retained untranslated per the central survivor-name cluster; etymology glossed at its first occurrence (II ii 1) and here. See `atrahasis-name-exceedingly-wise-atrahasis`.

i18n.en: He gathered the elders to his gate.
Atra-ḫasīs opened his mouth
and addressed the elders:
"My god is at odds with your god;

notes.official: Atra-ḫasīs's speech to the elders (III ii 14–16) is a cover-story that preserves Enki's oath-technicality: 'my god is at odds with your god; Enki and Enlil have grown angry with each other, and I have been driven out of your land.' It is literally true (Enki and Enlil ARE at odds) while concealing the Flood — the human counterpart to Enki's own indirection through the reed wall. Rendered plainly.

i18n.en: Enki and Enlil have grown angry with each other,
and I have been driven out of your land."
Whatever he had he loaded upon her:
his flocks and his cattle he brought up into her,

lines.translit: iṣ-ṣú-ri ša-me-e ù bu-ú-la ša ṣe-ri

i18n.en: the birds of the heavens and the beasts of the field.
His family he brought into the boat.
They ate and ate, they drank and drank.
But he kept going in and coming out;
he could not sit, could not kneel,
his heart was broken, he was vomiting gall.
The face of the day changed.
Adad was roaring in the clouds.

notes.official: From here Adad appears in his NORMAL storm-god role — the instrument of the Flood (*Adad išaggum ina erpeti* 'Adad was roaring in the clouds', III ii 27, 31) — the inverse of his rain-withholding drought-role in Tablet II (II iii 7). Carried by the central `adad-hadad-baal-storm-god-flood-instrument-cross-corpus`; the Tablet-II inversion is documented at the overlay `adad-inverted-drought-role-scope-note-atrahasis`.

i18n.en: He heard the sound of him,
and brought pitch to seal his door.
When he had bolted his door,
Adad was roaring in the clouds.
The winds were furious as he rose;
he cut the mooring-rope and set the boat adrift.

segments.label: The Flood breaks: Anzû rends the sky, the deluge comes upon the peoples like a battle, and Enki's heart breaks (Lambert–Millard III iii, curated)

preceding_lacuna.text: The column break between III ii and III iii falls in a damaged span; the opening lines of III iii are fragmentary and are not reconstructed here.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection: the fragmentary opening of column III iii is not reconstructed in this draft.]
Anzû was rending the sky with his talons.
He shattered the land like a pot, [and stilled] its clamor.

notes.official: *[māta] kīma karpatim rigimša išḫuṭ* 'he shattered the land like a pot, [and stilled] its clamor' (III iii 7): the Flood's stated PURPOSE is to silence the *rigmu* — the very clamor of humankind that set the whole cycle in motion (II i 3–7). The sound-frame closes here. The line is reconstruction-uncertain (the sign values and the exact simile are pending collation); the sense is well-attested. See `rigmu-huburu-clamor-of-overpopulation-flood-cause-atrahasis`.

i18n.en: The Flood came forth against the peoples.

notes.official: *[ibaʾ] abūbu eli nišī* 'the Flood came forth against the peoples' (III iii 8). *abūbu* (CAD A/1 77) is the poem's title-catastrophe, carried by the central `a-ma-ru-abubu-mabbul-great-flood-vocabulary-cross-corpus` (with Sumerian *a-ma-ru* and Hebrew *mabbûl*); its Akkadian-side `appliesTo` activation on the Atra-ḫasīs occurrences (iii 8, 12, 15; v 35, 36, 47; vi 21, 23; viii 10, 16) is flagged for the central step. Rendered 'the Flood'.

lines.translit: ki-ma qá-ab-li e-li a-wi-lu-ti i-ba-aʾ e-mu-uq-šu
lines.cuneiform: 𒆠𒈠 𒀊𒇷 𒂊𒇷 𒀀𒉿𒇻𒋾 𒄿𒁀𒀪 𒂊𒈬𒊌𒋗

i18n.en: Its might came upon the people like a battle.
One man could not see another;
they could not be recognized in the catastrophe.
The Flood bellowed like a bull;

notes.official: *abūbu kīma lî išappu* 'the Flood bellowed like a bull' (III iii 12) answers, word for word, the swelling population that 'bellowed like a bull' in II i 2 (*mātu kīma lî išappu*): the sound the Flood makes is the sound it was sent to end.

i18n.en: the wind shrieked [like] a screaming eagle.
The darkness was total; there was no sun.
The gods were afraid at the roar of the Flood.

notes.official: *ilū iptalḫū ana rigim abūbi* 'the gods were afraid at the roar of the Flood' (III iii 15). Note *rigmu* here denotes the ROAR of the deluge, not the human clamor of Tablet II — a homonym deliberately excluded from the scope of `rigmu-huburu-...`; the terror of the gods at their own instrument prepares their remorse (iii 16–17) and their hunger (iv 16–19).

i18n.en: Enki's heart was in torment within him,

notes.official: *Enki uštannaḫ libbašu … marūšu nadû maḫruššu* 'Enki's heart was in torment, for he saw his children cast down before him' (III iii 16–17): the wisdom-god's private anguish over the destruction of humankind — his own handiwork. The gods' REGRET at the loss of the beings they made (and depend on) is stated openly in the Akkadian and is rendered plainly; carried in part by the central `enki-deliberates-in-his-own-heart-...` entry. The interpretive Elohim-frame reading (the makers grieving an engineered creation) is escalated to the Explainer, not the line.

i18n.en: for he saw his children cast down before him.

segments.label: Nintu / Bēlet-ilī wails for her offspring, who fill the sea like dragonflies; the gods, cut off from offerings, hunger and thirst (Lambert–Millard III iii–iv, curated)

i18n.en: Great Nintu was biting her lips.

notes.official: The birth-goddess laments in her several names — *Nintu* (iv 4), *Bēlet-ilī* (iv 5), later *Mami* — biting her lips and 'weeping her weeping', the divine-feminine flood-lament carried by the central `inana-laments-her-people-...` and the birth-goddess cluster. Her grief is maternal: the drowned are the offspring she fashioned in Tablet I.

i18n.en: Bēlet-ilī wept her weeping.
"Like dragonflies they have filled the river!

notes.official: *kīma kulīlī imlaʾ nāram* 'like dragonflies they have filled the river' (III iv 6): the corpses of humankind compared to the ephemeral *kulīlu* (CAD K 505, 'dragonfly / mayfly'), the short-lived insect — an image both of teeming numbers and of the brevity of the life just extinguished. The second simile (iv 7, 'like a raft they have driven onto the shore') is reconstruction-uncertain. Rendered plainly.

lines.translit: ki-ma a-mi-im i-na ṣe-ri ir-ta-ak-bu a-na ki-ib-ri
lines.cuneiform: 𒆠𒈠 𒀀𒈪𒅎 𒄿𒈾 𒍢𒊑 𒅕𒋫𒀝𒁍 𒀀𒈾 𒆠𒅁𒊑

i18n.en: Like a raft they have driven onto the open shore.
I have looked upon them and wept over them;
I have exhausted my weeping for them."
She wept and gave vent to her heart;
the gods wept with her for the land.
She was sated with grief and thirsted for beer.
The gods' lips were parched with hunger.

notes.official: The consequence the gods did not foresee: with humankind destroyed, the offerings cease, and *ṣamû šaptašunu ilū ina bubūti* 'the gods' lips were parched with hunger' (III iv 16); the Anunna 'sat in thirst and hunger' (iv 18–19). Humankind was made in Tablet I to feed the gods through offerings (the *dullu*/service economy); the Flood severs that supply, and the makers starve — the mechanism that will make them swarm 'like flies' over the first post-flood sacrifice (v 41–42). Stated plainly in the Akkadian; the *bubūtu* is the same 'hunger/famine' lexeme used of humankind's afflictions in Tablet II (see `population-control-afflictions-vocabulary-atrahasis`).

i18n.en: The Anunna, the great gods,
sat in thirst and hunger.

segments.label: Seven days and seven nights; the Flood recedes; Atra-ḫasīs offers, and the gods gather over it like flies (Lambert–Millard III iv–v, curated)

preceding_lacuna.text: The intervening span of Nintu's lament and the passage of the storm (III iv 20 – III v 33) is compressed; the draft resumes at the seven-day span and the sacrifice.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection: the remainder of Nintu's lament and the passage of the storm (III iv 20 – III v 33) are compressed in this draft.]
For seven days and seven nights

notes.official: *ūm 7-kam u mūši 7* 'for seven days and seven nights' (III v 34) the Flood rages — the SEVEN-day duration of the Mesopotamian tradition (so Gilgamesh XI), against the FORTY days of Genesis 7:12. Carried by the central `seven-day-flood-vs-forty-day-flood-duration-tradition-cross-corpus`.

i18n.en: the Flood went on, the [tempest] overwhelming.
Then the tempest grew still, the Flood ceased.
[Atra-ḫasīs] came forth,
he set out an offering [to the gods],
he presented a sacrifice before the gods.
The gods smelled the savor;
like flies they gathered over the offering.

notes.official: *kīma zumbī eli niqî iptaḫrū* 'like flies they gathered over the offering' (III v 41–42): the starved gods swarm the first post-flood sacrifice. This is the OLDEST witness of a simile that recurs, nearly verbatim, at Gilgamesh XI 161–163 (*kīma zumbê … iptaḫrū*, the gods gathering over Ūta-napišti's offering) and stands behind — and in pointed contrast to — Genesis 8:21, where God smells the *rêaḥ nîḥōaḥ*, the 'pleasing aroma', with no unseemly swarming. The simile lays bare the offering-dependency: the gods gather because they are famished. Rendered literally ('like flies'); softening is refused, the indignity is the point. Carried by the central `gods-like-flies-vs-pleasing-aroma-flood-sacrifice-cross-corpus`, whose Akkadian-side `appliesTo` activation on this line is flagged as the older witness.

i18n.en: After they had eaten the offering,
Nintu arose to complain against all of them:
"Where has Anu, the lord of counsel, gone?

notes.official: Nintu's rebuke names Anu 'lord of counsel' (*bēl ṭēmi*) and Enlil, and charges that they *ša lā imtalkū-ma iškunū abūbu* 'without deliberating, brought on the Flood' (III v 47) and 'consigned the peoples to catastrophe' (v 48). The complaint that the destruction was rash and undeliberated sets up Enki's counter-proposal of measured checks (vi 19–24). Note *ṭēmu* here again in its 'counsel/deliberation' sense (cf. II vii 1), not the anthropogonic pun.

i18n.en: Has Enlil come near the incense —
they who, without deliberating, brought on the Flood
and consigned the peoples to catastrophe?"

segments.label: Enlil rages that a human survived; Enki confesses and defends his stratagem, and proposes measured checks in place of a flood (Lambert–Millard III vi, curated)

i18n.en: When Enlil saw the boat,

notes.official: Enlil's fury that the Flood was survived (III vi 5–10, 'when Enlil saw the boat … how did a man survive the catastrophe?') drives the poem's resolution. His outrage is that the oath was evaded; Anu at once names the only possible agent — 'Who but Enki could do such a thing?' (vi 13).

i18n.en: he was filled with fury at the Igigi:
"We, all the great Anunna,
together imposed an oath.
Where did life escape?
How did a man survive the catastrophe?"
Anu opened his mouth
and addressed the warrior Enlil:

lines.cuneiform: 𒈠𒀭𒉡𒌝𒈠 𒊭 𒆷 𒀭𒂗𒆠 𒄿𒅁𒁍𒋗 𒀀𒉿𒌓

i18n.en: "Who but Enki could do such a thing?

notes.official: Anu's 'Who but Enki could do such a thing?' (III vi 13) draws Enki's defense — 'I did not reveal the command of the gods' (vi 14, spoken as the accusation Enki turns aside) and then his open confession, 'I did it, indeed, against your will! I saw to it that life was preserved' (vi 17–18). The defense rests on the reed-wall technicality of III i 11: Enki warned the wall, not the man, and so did not 'reveal' the oath-bound decree. See `igaru-kikkishu-reed-wall-oath-loophole-atrahasis`.

i18n.en: I did not reveal the command of the gods."
Enki opened his mouth
and addressed the great gods:
"I did it, indeed, against your will!
I saw to it that life was preserved.
Lay the penalty on the wrongdoer,

notes.official: Enki's constructive proposal is the poem's turn from annihilation to management: rather than punishing all humankind collectively, 'lay the penalty on the wrongdoer' (III vi 19–20), and 'instead of your bringing on a Flood' let graduated checks — a lion, a wolf, famine, plague — 'diminish the peoples' (vi 21–24). The one-off total Flood is replaced by standing, proportionate population-controls, preparing the permanent limits Nintu institutes in column vii. The *bubūtu* famine reappears here as a recurring check (vi 24).

i18n.en: and his punishment on the transgressor.
Instead of your bringing on a flood,
let a lion arise and diminish the peoples.
Instead of your bringing on a flood,
let famine arise and let the land waste away."

segments.label: In place of another Flood: Nintu establishes non-bearing women, the pašittu-demon, celibate priestess classes, and settled mortality (Lambert–Millard III vii, curated)

preceding_lacuna.text: The transition from Enki's proposal of measured checks (lion, wolf, famine, plague) to his instruction to Nintu (III vi 25 – III vii 0) is compressed; the draft resumes at the establishment of the permanent human limits.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection: the transition to the establishment of the human limits (III vi 25 – III vii 0) is compressed in this draft.]
Enki opened his mouth
and addressed Nintu the birth-goddess:
"You, birth-goddess, creatress of destinies,
establish death for the peoples. [ … ]

notes.official: *šukni mūta ana nišī* 'establish death for the peoples' (III vii 4) is the etiological climax: humankind, made in Tablet I to be a near-perpetual labor-force, is now made permanently MORTAL so its numbers are self-limiting. *mūtu* is read as the CONDITION of mortality (the verdict), not a personified death-demon on the model of the *pašittu* two lines on — the plural etiological frame supports the condition-reading. Compare the mortality-verdicts of Adapa and Genesis 3:19 ('to dust you shall return'); carried cross-corpus by the central `return-to-the-earth-mortality-verdict-adapa-genesis-cross-corpus`, Akkadian-side activation flagged. See `mutu-settled-mortality-etiological-verdict-atrahasis`.

i18n.en: Furthermore, let there be among the peoples
the woman who bears and the woman who does not bear.

notes.official: *ālittu u lā ālittu* 'the woman who bears and the woman who does not bear' (III vii 7): barrenness is instituted as a permanent human category, the first of the standing fertility-checks. Rendered plainly; see `la-alittu-non-bearing-women-population-limit-atrahasis`.

i18n.en: Let there be among the peoples the pašittu-demon,

notes.official: *pašittu* (CAD P 253, probably from *pašāṭu* 'to blot out') is a demon of the birth-chamber, established 'to snatch the baby from the lap of her who bore it' (III vii 8–9) — the mythic aetiology of infant mortality and stillbirth, a deliberate check on human numbers. Retained transliterated with a descriptive gloss, following the Tablet-I precedent for technical keywords (*lullû*, *eṭemmu*). See `pasittu-infant-snatching-demoness-population-limit-atrahasis`.

i18n.en: to snatch the baby from the lap of her who bore it.
Establish the ugbabtu, entu, and igiṣītu priestesses:

notes.official: The population-limit apparatus closes with three celibate cultic classes — the *ugbabtu*, the *ēntu*, and the *igiṣītu* priestesses — placed under an *ikkibu* 'taboo' on childbearing: *lu ikkibū-ma alāda pursi* 'let them be under taboo, and so cut off childbirth' (III vii 10–11). Historically these lines are the mythic charter for real Old Babylonian institutions of childless priestesses (the *nadītu* and kindred classes), here retrojected as a divinely-instituted brake on population. Office-names retained transliterated; *ikkibu* rendered 'taboo'. See `ugbabtu-entu-igisitu-celibate-priestesses-ikkibu-birth-taboo-population-limit-atrahasis`.

i18n.en: let them be under taboo, and so cut off childbirth."

segments.label: The flood-song doxology and colophon (Lambert–Millard III viii, curated)

preceding_lacuna.text: The remaining lines of III vii and the opening of III viii are not reconstructed here; the draft closes with the poem's concluding doxology.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection: the close of III vii and the opening of III viii are not reconstructed in this draft.]
This song [ … ]

notes.official: The poem closes with its own doxological colophon (III viii 9–17): 'This song …', naming itself *zamār abūbi* 'the song of the Flood' (viii 16) and calling on the Igigi to hear and extol Enlil's greatness. The self-naming marks Atra-ḫasīs as a composed 'flood-song' (*zamāru*), the Mesopotamian flood-narrative in its oldest connected form. The final imperative *šimeā* 'Listen!' (viii 17) returns the hearer to the reed-wall's opening 'listen closely to me' (i 11), closing the frame.

i18n.en: we [brought] the Flood upon all the peoples,
yet a man survived the catastrophe.
You, counsellor of the gods, [the warrior],
at your command I brought a battle into being.
For your praise let the Igigi hear it,
let them extol your greatness to one another.
I have sung of the Flood to all the peoples:
Listen!"
